requiredCopiedValues: Students read values from the on-screen evidence tables while answering the native Buzz questions.
evidenceRequirements.missingEvidenceAction: Use the on-screen evidence table and route contradictory or unverifiable written responses to human review.

humanReviewTriggers: Student response conflicts with the on-screen evidence table.
Student reports values that fall outside the expected range but the recorded evidence may support them.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student uses valid alternative vocabulary or reasoning not covered by the model answer.
Student answer is blank, copied from the prompt, or too vague to verify.
Student cites no data when the prompt requires their own recorded values.

questions.prompt: Choose one fork and report all three of your recorded lengths for it. Use those three numbers as evidence to describe the pattern in the resonant lengths, and explain what that pattern shows about how successive standing waves fit inside this pipe.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on reporting your own three measured lengths, describing the pattern between them, and explaining that pattern with nodes, antinodes, and quarter wavelengths.

criteria: Reports the fork frequency and its three measured lengths; states that the 3rd and 5th lengths are about three times and five times the 1st; and explains that each successive resonance adds another half-loop while keeping a node at the water and an antinode at the rim, so the pipe holds an odd number of quarter wavelengths.
Reports the three lengths and notices they are roughly multiples of the first, but gives limited or vague reasoning about nodes, antinodes, or quarter wavelengths.
Reports no data, misreads the pattern, or gives reasoning unconnected to standing waves.

commonMisconceptions: Thinks successive resonances are evenly spaced rather than odd multiples.
Describes the pattern without reference to nodes or antinodes.
Confuses the air-column length with the wavelength itself.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your answer uses recorded evidence and connects it to the correct physics idea.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by adding the specific recorded values and completing the physics reasoning requested in the prompt.
feedback.noCredit: Return to the on-screen evidence, identify the values this question asks about, and explain them using the target concept.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the reasoning is unusual but could be correct, or if cited values disagree with the on-screen evidence.

questions.objective: wave speed is a medium property
questions.prompt: Your 12 trials used four different frequencies and twelve different air-column lengths, yet all 12 speeds came out close to the same value. Explain why, then account for the size of your percent difference.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on explaining why the speed did not change across four frequencies, citing your own speed values, and accounting for your percent difference.

criteria: Explains that wave speed is a property of the medium - set by the air and its temperature - not by the source, so changing the fork changes frequency and wavelength together in a way that leaves v = f(lambda) unchanged; cites the near-constant speeds or the average from the data table as evidence; and attributes the percent difference to measurement precision in locating each intensity peak rather than to a real change in the speed of sound.
Correctly states that the speed depends on the medium and cites some data, but does not account for the percent difference or confuses precision with a physical change.
Claims the speed depends on frequency, claims the differences prove the speed changed, or cites no data.

commonMisconceptions: Believes a higher-frequency source makes sound travel faster.
Treats the spread in calculated speeds as proof the speed of sound changed.
Attributes the percent difference to a mistake rather than to measurement precision.
